historical_timeline.summary: Born Rocco Francis Marchegiano in Brockton, Massachusetts.
Pneumonia as a small child; not expected to survive.
Drafted into the Army; takes up boxing; discharged in March 1946.
By one account, fighting from now on with a ruptured disc in his back.
Marries; a daughter and later an adopted son.
An arthritic right elbow from about this year.
Wins the world heavyweight championship in Philadelphia.
Announces his retirement as undefeated champion, 49-0, at 32; broken hands, back injuries and cuts during his career.
Back pain while playing at home; a hospital diagnoses a ruptured disc.
Hosts a weekly boxing program on television; later works as a referee and commentator.
Killed in a small-plane crash near Newton, Iowa, on the eve of his 46th birthday.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a retired professional boxer: a 32-year-old former heavyweight champion, four months retired, comes in a few weeks after a lumbar disc herniation with sciatica, on a background of years of back pain, with an aching thumb base from an old fracture. The episode covers the history and neurological examination of low back pain with radiculopathy and its red flags; when imaging and surgical referral are and are not needed; exercise therapy, motor control training and a short NSAID course without opioids under the 2017 American College of Physicians guideline; post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the thumb base with a splint, hand therapy and topical diclofenac under the 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation guideline; NSAID safety, with dyspepsia that follows unmonitored daily naproxen and its test-and-treat management; a brain health baseline after repetitive head impacts (symptom inventory, MoCA, mood, anxiety and sleep, no imaging without an indication, and traumatic encephalopathy syndrome as a research diagnosis); the metabolic change after a sudden end to heavy training, with weight, blood pressure confirmed by home readings, lipids and an exercise prescription; and anxiety screening that is negative.

visit_schedule.purpose: Establishing primary care after retirement from professional boxing: low back pain and left leg pain after a recent disc herniation, left thumb pain, weight gain and blood pressure after stopping training, a brain health baseline, mood, anxiety and sleep, and a sports medicine consultation

Same-day sick visit for epigastric pain on naproxen
Eight-week review: back pain after six weeks of physical therapy, the thumb splint, the stomach after stopping naproxen, weight and blood pressure
Twelve-week review: back and thumb on home programs, weight, blood pressure, mood, anxiety and sleep, and the plan ahead

hpi.narrative: Mr. Marciano returns two weeks after intake and was seen this morning by Dr. Achterberg-Lund of sports medicine. The pain down his left leg now comes only after sitting for an hour, and the numbness on the top of his left foot is less. His back aches at about 5 out of 10, stiff in the morning. He took naproxen twice a day for the first week and now takes it once a day after walking, with food, with no stomach upset. He uses the gel on his left thumb three times a day, and gripping is still sore. He took his blood pressure at home twice a day for a week as shown, and the average was 126/78 mmHg. He walks for an hour each morning and has not run or hit the bag. He has eaten smaller portions and his weight is down by 0.4 kg. He has no headaches, memory trouble or problems with balance, and is sleeping better than he was at intake.

assessment.assessment: An improving left L5 radiculopathy with no motor deficit and no red flags. Most such herniations improve within six to twelve weeks without surgery, and repeat imaging would not change the plan. A surgical opinion would be needed for any new weakness, saddle numbness or bladder or bowel change (the same day), or for disabling leg pain that has not improved after six to twelve weeks of good conservative care

assessment.display: Exercise therapy and return to training
assessment.assessment: Exercise therapy is the main treatment for both the radiculopathy and the chronic back pain: directional preference (extension) exercise, which centralizes his pain today, then motor control and progressive trunk and hip strengthening, twice a week for six weeks, then a home program. Naproxen with food is reasonable for a short course but should be needed less as therapy works; if he needs it most days he should say so rather than keep taking it. No opioids or muscle relaxants. Walking and swimming now; slow jogging on the flat once the leg pain has been gone for a few weeks; no heavy lifting from the floor for three months

Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left first carpometacarpal joint. A hand-based thumb orthosis has the strongest support and was fitted today, to wear for gripping work and at night, with hand therapy exercises and continued topical diclofenac. A corticosteroid injection is an option if pain persists after six to twelve weeks of this; it is not needed now

A normal baseline: no cognitive, mood, behavioral, sleep or balance complaints, a normal neurological screen, MoCA 29, PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4 and a PROMIS sleep T-score of 55 with back pain at night. Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis under the 2021 NINDS consensus criteria, which require progressive core clinical features; he has none, and the diagnosis is not made on a history of exposure alone. Brain imaging is not indicated without new symptoms or signs. The baseline should be repeated yearly, with earlier review for any change in memory, mood, behavior, speech or movement; he should avoid sparring and other head impacts

His current home average of 126/78 mmHg is in the elevated range and should improve with this
